raw_response:
# Existing mechanisms for controlling descriptor inheritance

Nine useful candidates emerged from the public searches. The descriptor-level mechanisms are relevant across multiple execution paths because the operating system applies their settings when exec succeeds. Launch-time cleanup and explicit descriptor mapping add useful controls, but their reach depends on which launchers use them.

1. **FD_CLOEXEC per-descriptor inheritance control** — https://man.openbsd.org/OpenBSD-5.2/close.2  
   Setting FD_CLOEXEC on non-shared descriptors lets the operating system close them on successful exec regardless of which library or extension initiates that exec. It acts on exec rather than fork alone, and external code that creates an unmarked descriptor still needs to participate. Setting the flag after creation also leaves a concurrency gap. **Evidence:** archived OpenBSD 5.2 manual dated November 6, 2011, before the cutoff.

2. **O_CLOEXEC on open/openat** — https://man.openbsd.org/OpenBSD-5.3/open.2  
   Opening files with O_CLOEXEC supplies a constructor-level non-inheritance setting that avoids relying on one particular subprocess wrapper. Apply the policy wherever files are opened, including participating native extensions, while accounting for platform support. The supplementary Linux manual explains why a separate open-then-fcntl sequence can race with a concurrent fork and exec: https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html. **Evidence:** the OpenBSD 5.3 manual is dated January 19, 2013; the supplementary live Linux page has an unestablished publication date.

3. **pipe2(O_CLOEXEC)** — https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pipe.2.html  
   Creating both pipe endpoints with pipe2(O_CLOEXEC) prevents unrelated executed children from retaining an unintended pipe endpoint. A child intended to use one end still needs explicit mapping or inheritance handling, and support must be checked for the operating system. **Evidence:** the opened live manual contains POSIX.1-2024 material; this is later evidence, even though its history lists earlier Linux and glibc versions.

4. **socket(..., SOCK_CLOEXEC, ...)** — https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/socket.2.html  
   Adding SOCK_CLOEXEC when creating sockets extends descriptor-level inheritance control to networking resources created outside the subprocess API. Other descriptor-producing networking operations need their own review; changing this constructor does not establish their behavior. **Evidence:** verified live documentation, publication date unknown; the historical version mentioned in its text was not treated as a dated original source.

5. **dup3(..., O_CLOEXEC)** — https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/dup.2.html  
   Using dup3 with O_CLOEXEC keeps descriptor duplication from silently reintroducing inheritance after the original descriptor was protected. Ordinary dup/dup2 clear close-on-exec on a new duplicate, which can be useful for deliberate child redirection, so the intended behavior must be selected explicitly. Also account for dup3 rejecting identical old and new descriptor numbers. **Evidence:** Linux man-pages 6.19 with POSIX.1-2024 content, classified as later evidence.

6. **Go ForkLock and explicit retained-descriptor policy** — https://go.dev/src/syscall/exec_unix.go  
   Go's public ForkLock implementation provides a concrete fallback design that coordinates descriptor creation plus close-on-exec marking against fork while explicitly selecting descriptors for the child. Its reader/writer lock protects cooperating creation and fork paths, and the source prefers atomic operating-system primitives where available. Uncooperative external native code bypasses the lock, and potentially blocking open fallbacks retain a race in the documented design. **Evidence:** live code was opened and native unauthenticated code search succeeded; historical go1.1 source retrieval failed. Neither a 2009 copyright nor a May 2013 release announcement establishes the date of the retrieved implementation.

7. **closefrom(3) child cleanup policy** — https://man.openbsd.org/OpenBSD-5.2/closefrom.2  
   Calling closefrom with a lower bound of 3 in a controlled child launch path removes extra descriptors while preserving descriptor numbers 0, 1 and 2. This can contain already-open unmarked descriptors, but it also closes intentionally shared extra descriptors and must be incorporated into each relevant launcher. Platform support is a material constraint. Here, “3” is the argument; the cited function is documented in manual section 2. **Evidence:** archived OpenBSD 5.2 manual dated May 31, 2007, before the cutoff.

8. **POSIX spawn file actions** — https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/posix_spawn.3p.html  
   POSIX spawn file actions provide an explicit descriptor-mapping stage followed by close-on-exec processing, useful for specifying intentional child I/O separately from ambient parent descriptors. The standard separately addresses descriptors 0, 1 and 2. It still permits unmarked descriptors to remain open, and it covers only launch paths that use this interface. **Evidence:** the opened specification is POSIX.1-2017, classified as later evidence; the requested historical Open Group page returned 403.

9. **GLib spawn descriptor and standard-stream flags** — https://docs.gtk.org/glib/flags.SpawnFlags.html  
   GLib's spawn flags demonstrate a concrete launch API that closes extra descriptors by default and exposes separate controls for inheriting standard streams. The LEAVE_DESCRIPTORS_OPEN option changes the handling of additional descriptors; standard input has its own inheritance option. This is a useful API example, but it only protects launches routed through GLib. **Evidence:** current GLib 2.91.0 documentation generated with gi-docgen 2026.1, classified as later evidence; later flags should not be assumed available in 2013.

For the supplied problem, the practical transfer is to cover descriptor creation and duplication across the runtime, preserve explicit standard-stream and extra-descriptor choices at launch, and identify which external modules remain outside that policy. A shared fallback lock requires cooperation; a cleanup function used in one launcher requires adoption by the other launchers.

**Search and evidence limits:** I made 9 search queries and 20 open attempts, counting both native code-search endpoints as opens; 14 opens succeeded and 6 were blocked. Public unauthenticated grep.app search returned HTTP 200, so native code search succeeded. Four prohibited proposal snippets or mirrors appeared in broad search results and were excluded without opening; prior model familiarity with the topic was also recorded as a recognized-memory exposure. No excluded proposal page was opened. Later and undated evidence is labeled above, and no deployment or effectiveness claim is made.
